Diego Velazquez. The Spanish Baroque master and one of the greatest painters of the seventeenth century, celebrated for his sophisticated handling of light, his penetrating court portraiture, and his enigmatic compositions that invite endless reinterpretation. As Philip the Fourth's favored painter, he elevated the portrait to a philosophical statement about perception, power, and artistic genius.

Velazquez painted Las Meninas in 1656, often called the greatest painting in Western art. It is simultaneously a scene of the royal court, a portrait of the artist, a reflection on the nature of seeing, and a meditation on artistic authority and surveillance. He was a master of tonality—using subtle shifts of muted color and tone rather than bold contrast to create luminosity and depth. His restraint gives his works a mysterious, contemplative quality.

From 1623 until his death, he served Philip the Fourth of Spain. He painted the king obsessively, dozens of portraits across the royal aging, achieving psychological penetration rarely seen in court painting. His early bodegan paintings—kitchen scenes—show humble Spanish life with the dignity and sophistication usually reserved for noble subjects. A radical democratization of subject matter.

Velazquez traveled to Italy twice, absorbing Venetian colorism and Roman Baroque grandeur. But his mature style is distinctly Spanish—reserved, philosophical, inward-turning. He was influenced by Caravaggio and the Spanish tradition of tenebrist realism, though his chiaroscuro is subtler than Caravaggio's. Less dramatic, more psychologically complex. His late works become increasingly loose and abstract. Faces dissolve into gestural brushwork, anticipating modern painting. His late self-portraits assert his artistic mastery and dignity, reaching similar psychological depth to his great contemporary Rembrandt.
